identity.title: High-dimensional Analysis of Synthetic Data Selection

problem.claim: Determine which properties of synthetic data influence classifier generalization error, studied through high-dimensional regression.

gap.claim: Beyond heuristics such as similarity to the real-data distribution, the specific properties affecting generalization error are unclear.

contributions.claim: For linear models, the authors characterize covariance shift as affecting generalization error, while mean shift does not.
They prove that covariance matching is optimal in some regimes and report that the linear-model insights carry over to deep neural networks and generative models.
They evaluate covariance matching against several recent synthetic-data selection approaches across training paradigms, datasets, and augmentation generative models.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors' stated distinction is the finding that covariance shift matters for linear-model generalization whereas mean shift does not, together with its reported carryover to deep neural networks and generative models.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report theoretical results separating the effects of covariance and mean shift on linear-model generalization error.
The authors report a proof that matching the target covariance is optimal in some regimes.
The authors report that covariance matching performs well against several recent selection approaches across varied paradigms, datasets, and generative models.

narrative_sequence.summary: Synthetic data have uncertain value for improving classifier prediction performance.
Existing guidance emphasizes distributional closeness but does not identify which data properties control generalization error.
The paper studies the question using high-dimensional regression and finds distinct roles for covariance and mean shift in linear models.
Covariance matching is proved optimal in some regimes, and the authors state that the insights extend to deep neural networks and generative models.
Covariance matching is reported to perform well against recent selection methods under varied augmentation settings.

source_observation.claim: The abstract isolates covariance shift and mean shift separately, then connects the theoretical distinction to a concrete covariance-matching procedure.

lessons.interpretation: Separating distributional factors can turn a broad data-quality heuristic into a testable selection rule.
lessons.application: When proposing a synthetic-data criterion, decompose distribution mismatch into explicit components and align each theoretical claim with a corresponding selection procedure.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the relevant mismatch cannot be represented by the chosen moments or when the target task is outside the analyzed model regimes.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the regimes in which covariance matching is optimal.
It does not report quantitative performance, baselines, datasets, training paradigms, or statistical uncertainty for the empirical comparisons.
The extent and conditions of the claimed carryover to deep neural networks and generative models are unspecified.
